title: Leather, scent and the sea
pair: Janbiya, incense, Taif rose, pearl divers · Blends, stretch and when polyester is fine

slides.title: Leather, scent and the sea
slides.text: Not all heritage is cloth. A dagger on a belt, smoke from a burner, a diver's leather finger guard. Today you collect the small things that make a garment feel Saudi, then learn when mixing fibers, even polyester, makes a garment better.

slides.q: What did the tiny bells on women's jewelry do?
options: Let people know a woman was near, so men looked away
slides.why: "Heard, but not seen." Move 13 turns it into a silent silver bead.
whys: The sources tie the bells to people, not animals.
They were worn every day, not just for dancing.
That wasn't their stated purpose.

options: The Najdi overdress's sheer cloth, full of tiny holes
slides.why: The sheer tulle overdress. Move 14 turns it into an open-weave overshirt for men.
whys: The name borrows a kitchen word, but it describes a dress.
It's a dress, not jewelry.
It's a dress, not a tent.

slides.q: Best silk for a summer abaya lining?
options: Light matte habotai or crepe under about 16 momme
slides.why: Light, matte, plain or crepe silk. Charmeuse is for evening.
whys: Charmeuse clings and shows sweat.
That's not silk, and it traps heat.
Twill is heavier.

slides.caption: A janbiya with a steel blade, bought in the souq of Sana'a, Yemen, in 1986.
slides.title: The janbiya: courage on the belt
text: The janbiya is a curved dagger worn at the front of a belt. In Najran it's made of iron or steel with a horn handle, often with silver or gold added. The best sheaths are inlaid with silver.
It stands for courage, manhood and tribe. When tribes make peace, they lay their daggers down. Many boys get their first one in their teens.
Najran's Al-Janabi souq is known for janbiya makers. Prices run from about 20 Saudi riyals (SR) to SR 250,000 or more.
src: Arab News: why the janbiya remains a symbol

slides.caption: Najran Fort (Emara Palace), Saudi Arabia.
slides.title: Najran's leather
text: Najran's leather workers made belts, a baby carrier (mezab) and big storage cases (zamalah). Hides came from camels, cattle, sheep and goats.
They tanned leather with plants. One plant (Calligonum) gave a light red. Another (St John's wort) gave a deep red.
Men wore the haskal: a money pouch under the left arm on a braided strap. Sandals had camel-skin soles and goat-skin tops.
slides.note: Plant-tanned leather is what luxury leather brands still sell today. It ages, darkens and softens. Najran was doing it with local plants.

slides.title: Smoke as a welcome

left.label: 2,400 years ago
left.caption: Stone incense burner from Yemen, 5th–4th century BCE (before the common era). Its inscription lists incense woods and resins.

right.label: Oud wood
right.caption: Top-grade agarwood, the wood burned as oud.

slides.takeaway: The mabkhara burns amber and oud on hot coals. The smoke scents the room, clothes, hair and guests. At weddings it's passed round so each guest can scent himself. In nine months of 2023–24, Saudi Arabia imported about 1.1 million kilograms of oud wood.

slides.caption: Picking Taif roses, 2026.
slides.title: Taif roses: picked before sunrise
text: Over 910 farms in Taif grow about 550 million roses a year. The bushes bloom only once a year, for 40 to 50 days.
Roses are picked early each morning, before the heat. Then they're distilled into rose water and oil.
Grades have names: al-Arus, "the bride's", is the strongest at about 80%. Then al-thanou at about 50%, and al-sayer at 20% or less.
src: Saudipedia: How Taif rose water is made

slides.caption: Arab pearl divers at work in the Gulf. From George Frederick Kunz, The Book of the Pearl (1908).
slides.title: The pearl divers of the east coast
text: On the Eastern Province coast, the main diving season lasted 130 days. Divers went down about 2 minutes at a time, to about 18 meters, around 50 times a day.
They wore sirwal shorts and a black shamshool, or cotton suits against jellyfish. A nose clip (fattam) was made of bone or horn. Leather finger covers (khabt) protected their hands from sharp rocks.
On a Saudi boat the catch was split: captain 20%, diver 40%, rope-puller 30%, helper 10%. Buyer and seller agreed a price by touching fingers under a red cloth.
slides.note: A secret price, agreed under a red cloth. That's a very quiet-luxury story.

slides.title: What the sea gave

left.label: The oyster
left.caption: A pearl oyster shell: rough outside, mother-of-pearl inside.

right.label: The work
right.caption: Divers and rope-pullers on the boat.

slides.takeaway: Rough outside, shining inside. That's the same idea as the roshan lining in Lesson 4 and the red-cloth deal: the beauty is hidden from the outside world. Mother-of-pearl buttons are a direct, honest nod to the divers.

slides.title: Two scents, two raw materials

left.label: Resin
left.caption: Frankincense resin, the tears of a tree.

right.label: Wood
right.caption: Oud: wood made dark and fragrant inside the tree.

slides.takeaway: Arabia traded incense for thousands of years. Scent belongs to how Saudis welcome guests. For a garment, keep scent on the packaging or a removable card, not baked into the cloth, so the customer chooses.

slides.caption: A spool of spandex (elastane) yarn.
slides.title: Now the fabric part: why mix fibers?
text: A blend mixes two or more fibers so each one adds what the others lack. The rule: every fiber must earn its place.
Elastane, also called spandex or Lycra, is a stretchy fiber. A little of it lets a woven fabric move with you.
Polyester in a blend can add strength and stop wrinkles. But it also lowers breathability, which matters a lot in Gulf heat.
src: Nona Source: why luxury uses synthetics

slides.title: Five blends, five reasons
slides.intro: Read each blend like a recipe: what each fiber adds, and who the blend is for.
layers: Tough, cheap, few wrinkles. Breathes less. Uniforms, not luxury.
Wool look with comfort stretch. Trousers, soft tailoring.
Cuts cost, adds toughness. High-street suits.
Wool stops linen wrinkling, silk adds shine, linen adds coolness. Loro Piana's summer cloth is 71% merino wool and 15% silk.
src: Bonne Gueule: Loro Piana wool, silk and linen

slides.title: How much stretch is too much?
slides.intro: Elastane percentage in a woven tailoring fabric.
slides.note: A 2024 study of suit fabrics found 7% or more elastane in the crosswise threads can make seams pucker. Knits for sport go much higher on purpose, but that's a different garment.
src: Journal of Natural Fibers (2024): elastane in suiting

slides.title: When is polyester fine?
slides.intro: Polyester is cheap when it replaces a better fiber. It's fine when it does a job natural fibers can't.

Fine.cap: Synthetic yarn on a spool (this one is spandex). Synthetics earn their place when they do a job.
items: on a coat, not against skin
Prada's Re-Nylon, from recycled fishing nets

Not fine.cap: Linen: what belongs next to the skin in Gulf heat.
items: In Gulf heat, it traps sweat
use cotton, linen, silk or fine wool

src: Nona Source: why luxury uses synthetics

slides.title: Move 16: The haskal pocket
slides.text: Najdi men kept money in a pouch under the left arm. Put a slim inside pocket in the same spot.
how: A slim inside pocket under the left arm of a jacket or coat, for a phone or cards.
Lined in plant-tanned leather, the light Calligonum red.
Women: the same pocket inside a long open coat.

slides.title: Move 17: The khabt tab
slides.text: Divers protected their fingers with small leather covers. Turn it into a small leather tab on a cuff or glove.
how: A small plant-tanned leather tab on a shirt or jacket cuff.
Tell the diver's story on the hangtag.

slides.title: Move 18: The red-cloth secret
slides.text: Pearl prices were agreed by touching fingers under a red cloth. Put that red where only the wearer sees it.
how: A deep red lining in a plain black or sand coat.
Pack each piece with an oud-scented card, not scented cloth (see the collar-pocket idea).

slides.title: Read three blend labels
slides.text: Find three garments with mixed fibers on the label.
checklist: Write each blend with its percentages
For each fiber, say what it adds
Judge it: luxury, mid-market, or workwear?
slides.notePrompt: Trousers: 52% wool, 46% polyester, 2% elastane. Wool adds..., polyester adds..., I'd call it...
context: Every fiber in a blend must earn its place. 65% polyester / 35% cotton is tough, cheap, and wrinkle-resistant but breathes less than cotton: uniforms, not luxury.
97% wool / 3% elastane gives comfort stretch for trousers. 2–3% elastane is normal in tailoring; a 2024 study found 7% or more can cause seam puckering.
Wool/silk/linen: wool stops linen wrinkling, silk adds shine, linen adds coolness; Loro Piana's 'Summertime' cloth is 71% merino wool and 15% silk.

Polyester is fine when it does a job natural fibers can't: holding a pleat, a weatherproof shell, a signature nylon with a story (Prada Re-Nylon from recycled fishing nets). Not next to the skin in Gulf heat.

slides.title: Design one leather detail
slides.text: Pick Move 16 or Move 17 and place it on a real piece you'd sell.
checklist: Choose haskal pocket or khabt tab
Say the leather color and why
context: The janbiya is a curved dagger worn at the front of a belt; in Najran it is iron or steel with a horn handle, often with silver or gold added. It stands for courage, manhood and tribe; when tribes make peace they lay daggers down.

Najran leather workers make the masbat (waist belt), mezab (baby carrier) and zamalah (storage case). Hides: camel, cattle, sheep, goat. Plant tanning gave light red (Calligonum) or deep red (St John's wort).
The haskal is a money pouch worn under the left arm on a braided strap. Divers wore khabt, leather finger covers, against sharp rocks.
Design ideas: a plant-tanned leather belt or strap with one small engraved silver piece; a slim inside pocket under the left arm like the haskal; a small leather tab on a cuff like the khabt.

slides.title: Plan the scent
slides.text: Decide how scent shows up when a customer opens an A'ila Areeqa box.
checklist: Pick the scent: oud, Taif rose or amber
Pick where: tissue paper, a card, or a collar pocket
Say why it's on the packaging, not in the cloth
slides.notePrompt: Scent: ___. Where: ___. Not in the cloth because...

refs.cap: Idea: a tiny collar pocket for a scent card.

context: The mabkhara is a charcoal incense burner: square base, sloping sides, metal-lined cup on top. Amber and oud wood are burned on hot coals; the smoke scents the room, clothes, hair and guests. At weddings it is passed round so each guest can scent himself.

Taif has over 910 farms growing about 550 million roses a year; the bush blooms once a year for 40–50 days and roses are picked early each morning. Al-Arus ('the bride's') rose water is about 80% strength.

Design ideas: wrap each garment in tissue lightly scented with oud bakhoor; a tiny collar pocket for a scent card; 'Al-Arus' as a hidden name on a label. Scent should be on packaging or removable cards, not baked into the cloth.

slides.q: What does the janbiya stand for?
slides.why: Courage, manhood and tribe. Tribes lay daggers down when they make peace.
whys: Silver on it can show wealth, but its meaning is bigger.
It's a dagger of honor, not a kitchen knife.
It's tribal and personal, not a religious rank.

slides.q: How did Najran craftsmen color leather red?
slides.why: With plants: Calligonum gave light red, St John's wort gave deep red.
whys: No paint: the color comes from tanning plants.
Rust wasn't used.
Raw hide isn't red. The plants made it red.

hint.cap: Look at the color of this leather.

slides.why: "The bride's" grade, about 80% strength. The best.
whys: That's al-sayer, at 20% or less.
It's made from Taif roses.
It's used for scent too, not only cooking.
src: Saudipedia: How Taif rose water is made

slides.q: How did pearl buyers and sellers agree a price?
options: Touching fingers under a red cloth
slides.why: Touching fingers under a red cloth, so nobody else knew. Move 18.
whys: The point was secrecy, not noise.
The deal was silent and hidden.
Not chance: a secret, careful deal.

slides.q: How much elastane is normal in tailored wool trousers?
slides.why: 2–3% gives comfort stretch. 7% or more can pucker seams.
whys: That's too little to feel.
10% is activewear territory and can pucker seams.
That's swimwear or leggings.
src: Journal of Natural Fibers (2024): elastane in suiting

slides.q: When is polyester a good choice for A'ila Areeqa?
options: Next to the skin in summer
For a heat-set pleat or a weatherproof outer shell
slides.why: When it does a job natural fibers can't: holding a pleat, or a weather shell.
whys: In Gulf heat it traps sweat.
Use cupro for linings (Lesson 4).
Faking a better fiber reads cheap.
src: Nona Source: why luxury uses synthetics

slides.title: Three things to keep
items: Najran: janbiya and plant-tanned red leather.
Move 16: the haskal pocket under the left arm. Move 17: the khabt tab.
Scent and pearls are about what's hidden.
Oud on the packaging, Taif's al-Arus as a hidden name, red inside like the pearl deal (Move 18).
Every fiber in a blend must earn its place.
2–3% elastane max in tailoring. Polyester only for pleats, shells, or a real story.
